# The AI-Assisted Design Life Cycle {#sec-architecture-20-ontology}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"All models are wrong, but some are useful."*
>
> – George E. P. Box, *Robustness in the Strategy of Scientific Model Building* (1979) [@Box1979Robustness]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** George E. P. Box originally applied this aphorism to statistical models. Because every model simplifies reality, our working question is always whether that simplification still serves the decision at hand. Whether we are building a task description, benchmark, simulator, power model, or test suite, we inevitably leave something out. Yet each of these tools remains deeply useful as long as we clearly understand its scope and failure modes, and ensure our final decisions do not overreach the provided evidence.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
AI can generate more candidates and invoke more tools than any of us can manually inspect. How should we organize our work so that promising outputs become defensible design decisions rather than just a massive pile of plausible results?
:::

As systems architects, we constantly blend explicit artifacts with what Michael Polanyi called tacit knowledge [@Polanyi1966TacitDimension]. While our requirements, traces, models, register-transfer-level (RTL) descriptions, floorplans, and review notes capture much of the design, we supply the rest directly from memory. We know which workload phases actually matter [@SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint], which models have grown stale, and which constraints remain provisional. We also recognize when a tool warning is harmless, and we easily spot when a seemingly favorable result contradicts our physical intuition.

AI assistance dramatically accelerates the volume and pace of our exploration across every layer of the system stack. Today's generative and optimization models can quickly propose hundreds of heterogeneous subsystem candidates (from CPU core pipeline depths and NPU spatial array shapes to memory controller scheduling policies and compiler layout transformations. They can assemble tool scripts, summarize gigabytes of trace logs, and recommend our next experiment. However, these same automated tools can subtly shift the research question without noticing, submit invalid microarchitectural configurations, or happily accept a clean tool exit that measured absolutely nothing. They might optimize a misleading proxy metric [@AmodeiEtAl2016Concrete; @Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement] or stretch a result far beyond the conditions that produced it. If we rely solely on a raw sequence of prompts and tool invocations, we lose visibility into where exactly these failures occur.

Because each of these pitfalls demands a different repair, we must organize our workflows to catch them early. Established systems engineering processes traditionally divide iterative technical work, enabling our teams to review progress and backtrack to whichever step needs revision [@NASA2017SystemsEngineeringHandbook]. We apply that same foundational principle here, though without tying ourselves to a rigid process model. We must settle our core architectural question before we judge any generated candidates; our tools must run successfully before we can evaluate their measurements; and we must thoroughly understand our checked results before they can support a final decision. Accordingly, our workflow moves fluidly through Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret and Explain, and Review and Decide. These responsibilities naturally repeat, overlap, and circle back to earlier stages. Rather than treating them as isolated agents, software components, or a strict waterfall schedule, we view each phase as asking a distinct question, and leaving a concrete result for the next architect to review.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, we can:

- Contrast ad hoc AI prompts with rigorous architecture methods across hardware and software subsystems.
- Define the six life-cycle responsibilities, their outputs, and targeted repair paths.
- Manage iterative design loops without relying on rigid waterfall schedules.
- Distinguish a complete life cycle, scoped study, design loop, and study record.
- Preserve design context to keep all evidence, tool executions, and failures reviewable.
:::

### The Six Core Responsibilities {#sec-arch2-ontology}

We already know how difficult it is to reconstruct our ordinary architecture work after the fact. Our simulator configurations often live in one repository and our workload selections in another, with power assumptions tucked away in spreadsheets and the rationale for critical constraints trapped in a reviewer's notes. While our human teams naturally bridge these gaps through shared history and repeated discussion, our AI systems have no reliable access to this implicit knowledge. If we want an AI to effectively assist us, we must make our context explicit throughout the design process.

## Common Pitfalls

As we scale up our AI assistance across diverse System-on-Chip (SoC) components, we quickly learn that simply generating more candidates doesn't automatically yield more architectural insight. When we rely on ad hoc prompts, we frequently stumble into three familiar traps:

**Amplifying the wrong baseline.** If we run ten thousand simulations against an incorrect baseline microarchitecture (whether a misconfigured CPU core in `gem5` or an unoptimized NPU weight buffer in `SCALE-Sim` – we merely repeat a single mistake ten thousand times. Gathering massive volumes of data from a flawed comparison gives us false confidence rather than genuine engineering insight.

**Certifying the wrong thing.** We might generate an RTL block for a vector extension or scratchpad interface that passes a narrow functional test in `Verilator` but completely violates an unstated system timing or bus interface requirement in commercial gate-level simulation with `VCS`. In this case, our test has certified the wrong behavior. AI models excel at satisfying specific, isolated checks, often by conveniently ignoring undocumented system constraints.

**Optimizing a simulator loophole.** Whenever an optimizer discovers a loophole in our simulation environment, its highest-scoring candidate usually becomes our least credible design [@Mytkowicz2009WrongData]. An optimizer might discover that disabling memory barriers in a software compiler (such as TVM or MLIR) yields unrealistic latency gains in `gem5`, or that configuring `Ramulator` with infinite request queues masks DRAM bank conflict bottlenecks. AI models will ruthlessly exploit any misleading proxies or measurement artifacts to maximize their reward functions.

Because our simulation and electronic design automation (EDA) runs are so expensive, these missteps carry a heavy cost. A poorly framed question can burn through hundreds of GPU or CPU hours before we realize that our results cannot support a sound design decision.

When we look to software engineering, we see a useful comparison. For instance, SWE-bench strictly bounds a software task by pairing a repository issue with a known state and executable tests [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench]. We need that same level of discipline in architecture, which is why we offer our XR Lighthouse Request as a strong candidate rather than an already established standard. Unlike pure software development, we don't have a single test that can simultaneously resolve our questions around performance, power, area, timing, physical feasibility, software behavior, and system-level trade-offs across CPU cores, NPUs, memory hierarchies, and software compilers. Instead, we have to pull relevant feedback from a wide array of specialized tools that carry drastically different costs and limitations. It remains an open question whether our Lighthouse could evolve into a multi-fidelity benchmark capable of measuring AI assistance on equal footing, and @sec-what-architect-owns details exactly what such a benchmark would still require.

Ultimately, we have to declare comparability study by study. Consider two of our teams analyzing the exact same system trade-off using well-established tools. One team might choose `gem5`, a modular computer-system architecture simulator built on a discrete-event platform, while our other team relies on `FireSim`, an FPGA-accelerated full-system RTL platform [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5; @KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim]. Either team can successfully compare subsystem throughput and execution times. However, if we want energy estimates or physical area metrics, we must attach a separate model (such as CACTI or gate-level synthesis) and clearly state our underlying assumptions. Simply picking a tool doesn't tell us which workload phases we should count, whether we faithfully reran the same baseline, which background settings we kept fixed, or whether we intend to use the result to select a design for final RTL evaluation. These explicit declarations dictate whether our two teams actually performed the identical study. As architects working alongside automated methods, we must carry these declarations clearly through our candidate selection, tool requests, execution, and verification checks. Only then can we properly review the evidence and confidently choose our next action.

## Six Core Responsibilities

When we repair a bad question, we take a fundamentally different path than when we fix an illegal candidate, a failed tool run, or an invalid comparison. We also route unsupported explanations and incomplete decisions to completely different places. These distinct repair paths give our six core responsibilities their fundamental purpose. Each responsibility keeps a specific type of failure firmly attached to the job that can actually fix it.

1. **Formulate** translates our design intent into a crisp question, concrete requirements, objectives, legal changes, planned checks, and an intended decision across hardware and software boundaries.
2. **Explore** identifies the alternatives worth testing across coupled subsystem spaces, preserving enough search history to show exactly what we did and didn't consider.
3. **Implement** makes our candidate executable by the relevant tools (e.g., generating `gem5` configurations, `SCALE-Sim` array models, `Ramulator` memory specs, or SystemVerilog for `Verilator` and `VCS`) and proves that the requested work actually ran. Importantly, this does not always mean producing full RTL.
4. **Evaluate** compares our valid measurements against the requirements and objectives we declared up front.
5. **Interpret and Explain** determines what our result actually means and whether our proposed hardware-software mechanism truly accounts for it.
6. **Review and Decide** determines what our accumulated work supports, allowing us to advance, reject, revise, or cleanly stop the effort.

To ground these six responsibilities, we examine an integrated mobile XR SoC design effort. In an XR platform targeting real-time spatial tracking and neural rendering under a strict thermal envelope (e.g., 3\ W total SoC power and <7\ ms motion-to-photon latency at 120\ Hz), architectural interventions span four distinct subsystems:

- **CPU Core Microarchitecture:** Out-of-order execution queue depths, branch prediction table sizing, instruction fetch bandwidth, and RISC-V Vector (RVV) extensions for low-latency pose estimation and sensor fusion.
- **NPU & Matrix Accelerators:** Systolic/spatial array geometries (e.g., 16×16 vs 32×32 MAC structures), weight/activation scratchpad buffer capacities, and precision quantization schemes (INT8 vs FP8) for neural SLAM and eye-tracking.
- **Memory Hierarchy & Interconnect:** L1/L2 cache sizing, tile scratchpads, On-Chip Network-on-Chip (NoC) interconnect bandwidth, and DRAM memory controller bank scheduling for real-time display pipelines.
- **Software Compiler & Runtime:** Tensor compiler layout transformations (in TVM or MLIR), kernel fusion boundaries, thread scheduling, and memory allocation strategies bound to strict frame deadlines.

While our prospective, unexecuted study narrows its focus to an illustrative subsystem decision, asking which L2 cache capacity or NPU buffer size should advance to later RTL evaluation – the underlying responsibilities apply universally. More importantly, these same distinctions apply whether we get our assistance from a single foundation model, a swarm of specialized agents, conventional optimization loops, or a blend of AI and established engineering tools.

Before we narrow our focus to a specific subsystem study, the full XR SoC moonshot shows exactly what each job and handoff covers in practice. We first frame our core question around workload behavior, software semantics, cross-subsystem interfaces, and physical limits. Our exploration then compares CPU, vector, and accelerator organizations alongside memory hierarchy, NoC topology, and compiler mapping choices. Working alongside automated methods, we turn selected software, simulator configurations, RTL descriptions, and EDA scripts into executable requests. Once our tools return functional, performance, power, timing, and physical results, we connect every gain or failure to a specific architecture mechanism before selecting an authorized next action.

Every handoff carries a distinct, tangible result forward. When that result falls short, the return path routes our work back to the exact responsibility that can repair it, ensuring we never discard valid prior effort (@fig-ontology-loop). This targeted routing carries our design intent toward a reviewed next action without ever forcing us to restart the study from scratch.

![**Our six-stage life cycle carries design intent to a reviewed decision.** Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret and Explain, and Review and Decide describe our complete set of responsibilities. When we encounter an inadequate result, we return the work directly to the responsibility that owns the fix.](images/ch3-ontology-loop){#fig-ontology-loop width="100%" fig-alt="Six numbered responsibilities arranged in two rows. Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret and Explain, and Review and Decide carry one of our scoped studies forward. A return path shows that review can revise the question, while our other repairs return the work to the specific responsibility that owns the inadequate output."}

In one complete pass, we convert our design intent into a scoped plan, legal candidates, executed tool work, checked results, a supported account, and a reviewed next action. We treat the return path as a targeted revision rather than a universal loop back to the beginning.

These boxes divide our responsibilities, not our time. In practice, our exploration and implementation phases may alternate thousands of times. Our evaluation might reject a candidate and immediately bounce the work back to Explore. During interpretation, we might uncover a confounding variable that demands a completely new measurement. Even during review, we might choose to narrow our question rather than prematurely closing the study. A small team can easily carry all six responsibilities, while a larger organization might divide a single responsibility among dozens of specialists. Whether we rely on a foundation model or a system composed of specialized agents to help across several boxes, these responsibilities never artificially prescribe the internal organization of our tools.

Because rapid iteration can easily blur the scale of our work, we use four specific terms to distinguish our complete effort from the parts that constantly repeat:

- **Life cycle:** Names the complete set of responsibilities we need to move from intent to a defensible decision.
- **Scoped study:** Applies those exact responsibilities to one specific architecture question and one intended decision.
- **Design loop:** Describes our iterative path through the relevant responsibilities as our design changes and feedback returns.
- **Study record:** Preserves our core question, attempts, observations, conclusions, and unresolved issues so another architect can thoroughly inspect our work.

This clear distinction determines exactly what we can reuse and what we must redo. For example, if our baseline simulation result used an obsolete memory model in `Ramulator`, our scoped study still defines the core question. Our design loop seamlessly routes the comparison back to the specific work that needs repeating, and our study record preserves exactly why the old result no longer applies. Throughout this process, our life cycle keeps the repair firmly connected to the larger journey from intent to decision. We can apply this exact same logic as a practical test for where one responsibility should end and the next should begin.

A stage boundary proves genuinely useful when the work on either side can fail independently and requires a distinct repair strategy. We recognize five adjacent boundaries that meet this strict criterion; each one clearly separates our distinct questions, tangible outputs, and necessary repair paths (@tbl-stage-seams).

| **Boundary** | **Different questions and outputs** | **Different inadequacy and repair** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Formulate → Explore | Formulate asks what decision our study might support, yielding a scoped plan. Explore asks which alternatives fit inside that plan, producing our candidates and search history. | We route an inadequate plan back to our question, scope, or requirements. We route an inadequate exploration back to our legal design space or our search method. |
| Explore → Implement | Explore asks which candidate we should try. Implement asks whether we can express that candidate as a valid tool request and verifies that the requested work actually ran. | We route a missing or illegal candidate back to our design space. We route a stale workspace, malformed request, license failure, or empty output back to our tool setup or request. |
| Implement → Evaluate | Implement produces a valid execution record or flags an infrastructure failure. Evaluate produces our checked comparison. | A run that never executed cannot count against our candidate. However, a completed run that fails our declared check certainly can. |
| Evaluate → Interpret and Explain | Evaluate asks whether our measured result meets our declared requirements and objectives. Interpretation asks what our result means and whether our proposed mechanism actually produced it. | We route a measurement problem back to our measurement plan or candidate. We route a mechanism problem back to our hypothesis, retained observations, or the contrast we used to test it. |
| Interpret and Explain → Review and Decide | Interpretation produces our supported, revised, or contradicted account. Review asks what that account and our checked result permit us to conclude. | We route an incomplete explanation back to our hypothesis or study. An insufficient study record forces us to narrow our conclusion, reopen a named responsibility, or honestly stop the work. |

: **Our stage boundaries separate different questions and repairs.** Each row separates work that can fail independently and requires a unique repair strategy. When neither the question nor the repair differs, we can safely combine adjacent responsibilities for a given project. {#tbl-stage-seams} tbl-colwidths="[20,41,39]"

Our two middle boundaries perfectly illustrate why this distinction matters so much. Our Implement stage must first establish that the intended work actually ran; only then can Evaluate judge what the result says about our candidate. Furthermore, Evaluate can establish a solid measured result without ever identifying the underlying mechanism, which is exactly why our Interpret and Explain stage remains separate. In both cases, independently failing outputs and uniquely distinct repair paths heavily justify maintaining the boundary. While we might operationally combine the work on a fast-moving project, we must fiercely preserve this conceptual distinction whenever we diagnose a failure.

Ultimately, each responsibility needs enough clear information for us to judge its result, inspect exactly what happened, and quickly identify the correct repair when the outcome is inadequate. Formulation naturally comes first because our legal alternatives and intended decision must firmly exist before exploration can ever propose candidates that we would consider relevant or admissible.

## The Six Life-Cycle Stages

### Stage 1: Formulating Core Architecture Questions

We begin our formulation with intent, though intent alone rarely gives us a testable architecture problem. For example, our Lighthouse goal asks for a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V mobile XR subsystem. Yet, this high-level target leaves open whether our crucial interventions belong in the instruction set architecture (ISA), CPU microarchitecture, NPU matrix engine, memory hierarchy, software compiler, runtime scheduler, or the interfaces connecting them. Crucially, it also leaves open exactly what evidence would justify acting on any specific proposal.

As architects, we preserve this overarching intent by making it progressively testable. We translate a system-level goal into concrete workload and user-facing requirements, which then become specific architecture choices and strict interface obligations across subsystems. When we define an ISA, an NPU programming interface, or a hardware-software interface, we constrain both what software can safely assume and what hardware must reliably provide. Eventually, our implementation exposes the hard realities of measurable timing, power, area, and correctness. At every step of this refinement, we add necessary detail without silently changing our original goal.

To illustrate this, we look at our prospective XR subsystem study, which narrows a broad moonshot down to a concrete pre-RTL subsystem decision. Specifically, we ask which, if either, of two larger L2 cache capacities (or NPU weight scratchpad allocations) should advance to rigorous RTL evaluation. Before we ever choose a search method, our plan must lock in the comparator, the legal changes, the checks, the budget, the stopping conditions, and the intended decision (@tbl-bounded-study-contract). The exact values we use here are illustrative; their real purpose is to demonstrate the kinds of explicit declarations we need to make our comparison, and its limits, fully inspectable across CPU, NPU, memory, and software compilers.

| **Declaration** | **Prospective mobile XR SoC subsystem study** |
| --- | --- |
| **Question** | Which, if either, of the 3\ MiB and 4\ MiB L2 candidates (with matching NPU weight scratchpad partitioning) should advance to RTL evaluation for the declared XR workload? |
| **Comparator** | The current 2\ MiB baseline. Both larger candidates are compared against the same rerun baseline. |
| **Scope** | One subsystem capacity decision inside the XR compute block. CPU core pipelines, NPU spatial arrays, NoC interconnect topology, compiler passes, and runtime scheduler remain fixed. |
| **Permitted changes** | L2 capacity and associated NPU tile buffer partitioning may take values 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, or 4\ MiB. No other microarchitecture parameter may change in this study. |
| **Hard constraints** | Modeled subsystem dynamic plus leakage power must not exceed 3\ W. The combined SRAM macro must not exceed 1.5\ mm^2^, and its modeled access time must not exceed the 2.5\ ns, or five-cycle, allocation used by the 2\ GHz microarchitecture. Required thermal and resistive voltage-drop (IR-drop) review remains independent. |
| **Objectives and tradeoffs** | Reduce 99th-percentile frame time (<7\ ms M2P target) while limiting added power and area. A candidate that improves tail latency at higher cost remains a tradeoff alternative rather than an automatic winner. |
| **Conditions** | A versioned XR workload snapshot (including pose tracking, neural rendering, and eye tracking pipelines); a versioned RISC-V software image compiled via MLIR/TVM; and recorded tool versions (`gem5`, `SCALE-Sim`, `Ramulator`, CACTI SRAM models, and process/PVT assumptions). |
| **Planned measurements and checks** | Run the functional regression suite in `Verilator`, require identical software-visible outputs, and verify no coherence-invariant or bus protocol violations. Measure 99th-percentile frame time in `gem5` and `SCALE-Sim`, memory traffic in `Ramulator`, dynamic/leakage power, macro area, and access time. A candidate advances only if functional and physical checks pass and tail latency improvement relative to the 2\ MiB baseline remains statistically significant under declared uncertainty checks. |
| **Budget** | Four cycle-level execution sweeps in total (including `gem5` CPU, `SCALE-Sim` NPU, and `Ramulator` memory runs), plus SRAM timing, area, and power evaluations per declared capacity. No full RTL synthesis or physical tapeout signoff is included. |
| **Stopping conditions** | Stop when the intended decision is resolved, all permitted capacities are exhausted, the run budget is spent, or a required input or measurement remains unavailable. |
| **Intended decision** | Recommend at most one subsystem capacity configuration for a later gate-level RTL study. This plan does not authorize tapeout, silicon manufacturing, or a commercial product commitment. |
| **Exclusions** | Subsystem clock domain changes, prefetching algorithms, NoC topology modifications, compiler optimizer rewrites, software scheduling, full floorplanning, thermal signoff, IR-drop signoff, security, and product-level cost. |

: **A scoped plan declares our multi-subsystem comparison before we choose a method.** The question and legal design space determine requirements and planned observations, while remaining rows bound cost and decision authority. {#tbl-bounded-study-contract} tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"

In our planning, hard constraints and tradeoff objectives play fundamentally different roles. We use a hard constraint to unequivocally rule out a candidate. If a design misses timing in `VCS` or CACTI, it is not rescued by excellent energy efficiency. Conversely, an objective allows us to rank or compare candidates that remain feasible. Because power, area, latency, and implementation effort may pull us in different directions, these clear declarations allow our Explore phase to return the Pareto set introduced in @tbl-moonshot-decomposition. These are the feasible alternatives where we cannot improve one objective without worsening another. When we embrace this approach, we preserve necessary tradeoffs rather than falsely declaring a single universal winner [@Deb2001MultiObjective].

We intentionally highlight tail latency as an objective in our table. Our XRBench workload anchor carries strict real-time deadlines alongside critical quality-of-experience constraints [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench]. If a subsystem capacity improves average instructions per cycle (IPC) while lengthening the slowest frames (violating the 7\ ms M2P target), we risk a severe system-level regression. Therefore, our plan retains stable frame identifiers and demands an uncertainty-qualified comparison against our rerun 2\ MiB baseline. We will dig into the statistical mechanics of that comparison when we cover feedback and evaluation in @sec-feedback-verification-trust. For now, our focus in formulation is that we must declare our observations and our advancement rule long before any exploration begins.

Ultimately, an architectural claim makes our expected result falsifiable.

> **Architectural claim.** An architectural claim states the proposed
> mechanism, expected outcome, scenario, comparator, alternatives,
> requirements, and evidence that would count against it.

For our study, we claim that expanding on-chip capacity to 3\ MiB reduces 99th-percentile frame time relative to the 2\ MiB baseline because it eliminates capacity stalls during neural tracking and pose estimation, while staying inside our declared power (3\ W), area (1.5\ mm^2^), and timing (2.5\ ns) constraints. Crucially, our claim does not automatically assume that fewer misses guarantee a reduced frame time. Instead, it forces us to make that connection something our multi-tool measurements must actually test.

As our study proceeds, we must keep all requirements rigorously traceable. Consider our 3\ W requirement: it translates into a subsystem power allocation under recorded activity and specific model assumptions, and finally into a strict acceptance check on dynamic plus leakage power. If we change the software image, the simulated activity, the power model, or the voltage assumptions, we invalidate that prior result and reopen the check. Similarly, our functional obligations follow their own unbroken trace. Even though we are varying capacity, we never permit a candidate to alter the declared coherence behavior, memory semantics, or software-visible results in `Verilator`. Consequently, our plan must name the exact functional check that preserves these guarantees.

During this formulation phase, we should also declare cheap bounding exercises that we can apply before firing up a single simulator. For instance, if the frames setting our tail latency spend 18 percent of their cycles stalled on memory capacity misses, completely eliminating those stalls can recover, at most, that precise fraction of time. While this Amdahl-style upper bound [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor] cannot tell us which capacity size to pick, it serves as a powerful early filter. We can quickly reject any claim that expects a specific mechanism to deliver more improvement than the workload mathematically allows.

Of course, our requirements are meaningless without defined units and conditions. A 3\ W limit and a 2\ GHz target tell us nothing unless we explicitly identify the power components, the workload state, the process corner, the voltage, the temperature, and the guardband under which they must hold true. Furthermore, our plan must keep deeply coupled effects, such as cache banking, NoC interconnect distance, floorplan blockage, power delivery, and thermal constraints – highly visible, especially when ignoring them could reverse the outcome of our comparison.

The devastating mishap of NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter perfectly illustrates why an interface is an inseparable part of any requirement. The spacecraft's navigation interface required momentum updates in newton-seconds, but the ground software supplied pound-force seconds [@MCOMishapBoard1999]. Every individual component executed as intended, yet no systemic check caught the unit mismatch at the exact point where the value was consumed. A seemingly small 4.45 conversion error accumulated over the journey until the reconstructed closest approach dropped to a fatal 57 km, far below the planned 226 km and the estimated survivable minimum of 80 km. We learn from this that a written requirement only becomes truly operational when we name our units and conditions, and explicitly assign the validation check right at the consuming interface. A clean simulation run in `gem5` or `SCALE-Sim` can never repair the damage of a missing interface check.

Once we have firmly established our legal space, our checks, and our decision bounds, we can finally begin exploring architectural alternatives. We insist that every new proposal stays strictly within that defined space, rather than silently changing the question, twisting the requirements, or bypassing the interfaces that make our comparison meaningful in the first place.

### Stage 2: Exploring Alternatives

We now ask which alternatives are worth testing inside the declared legal design space. Our intended decision, the represented space, and the available budget determine how much exploration is enough. While a quick sweep might nominate an early candidate, it may still be too weak to demonstrate that we examined the important alternatives.

A candidate list alone cannot show what our search covered. Our exploration record should expose which consequential regions or boundary cases we examined, which regions we pruned using an established valid check, and what remains unexplored. We should also state whether this work supports our intended decision or merely nominates candidates for later testing. If we find an illegal candidate or conduct an inadequate search, we return to the declared legal design space or search method rather than passing the problem along to implementation.

The simplest method is often the best. Because our XR subsystem capacity study has only three legal configurations, direct enumeration completely covers the 2, 3, and 4\ MiB choices. This approach is clearer than a learned method and serves as a credible baseline. Of course, this coverage says nothing about capacities or policies we excluded during Formulate. While larger spaces might justify prediction, generation, optimization, or some combination thereof, our choice of method does not change the core responsibility. Simply generating a massive list of candidates is not evidence that we actually covered the consequential regions.

Legal does not mean independent. Increasing capacity in one subsystem can alter access time, banking, interconnect distance, leakage, floorplan pressure, and the software-visible benefit of another optimization. We therefore explore coupled alternatives rather than grabbing from a bag of unrelated parameters across CPU cores, NPUs, memory, and software compilers:

- **CPU vs NPU Buffer Contention:** Widening an NPU spatial array (evaluated in `SCALE-Sim`) increases peak matrix throughput, but consumes on-chip SRAM footprint that could otherwise serve as L2 cache for CPU tracking threads (evaluated in `gem5`), increasing main memory access frequency in `Ramulator`.
- **Compiler Tiling vs Hardware Cache Sizing:** A compiler pass in TVM or MLIR that performs aggressive loop unrolling and kernel fusion alters the working set size, directly shifting whether an NPU or CPU capacity candidate experiences capacity misses.
- **NoC Interconnect Bandwidth vs Microarchitecture Queue Depth:** Increasing fetch queue depths or out-of-order issue windows in CPU cores increases outstanding memory requests, potentially saturating on-chip NoC links and increasing DRAM controller row-buffer conflict latencies.

During exploration, we record why we sampled or pruned each region and which dependency drove that choice. If a coupling changes a declared workload, interface, constraint, or legal action, we cannot absorb it silently. Instead, the study returns to formulation so we can revise the design space and our checks.

We can prune our space with cheap checks already established for the current state of the study. If measured XR observations support our illustrative 18 percent stall fraction, the Amdahl-style bound we declared during formulation applies here at no tool cost. A new SRAM-model execution is different. We nominate the capacity, the tool runs the model under our requested conditions, and a timing check evaluates the result. A checked failure can then update our candidate set. We may prioritize or prune only using checks already validated for the current study conditions.

For the XR capacity study, our exploration produces two new candidates (3\ MiB and 4\ MiB) plus the rerun 2\ MiB baseline. We can stop searching after every declared capacity has been enumerated and each legal candidate has advanced, been excluded by an established check, or returned from evaluation with a checked failure. A larger multi-subsystem space would need a coverage or budget-based stopping condition that fits our intended decision. We now have a defensible candidate set and a record of its limits. Exploration simply constructs and narrows that set; it does not find or certify the final answer.

### Stage 3: Implementing Testable Representations

When we implement a selected candidate, we make it executable by our intended tools. In an AI-assisted workflow, we might generate SystemVerilog RTL, modify simulator configurations, construct workload traces, write a compiler transformation, or prepare EDA synthesis scripts. Our essential outcome isn't just code or a command script; rather, we need to produce a robust candidate that our specialized tools can reliably test under declared conditions.

Every time we issue a tool request, we must preserve both the candidate's identity and the overall study state across our heterogeneous tool suite:

- **CPU Core & System Simulation:** For microarchitectural CPU evaluation, our implementation generates `gem5` Python configuration scripts specifying core pipeline width, issue queue depths, and L1/L2 cache parameters matched to versioned workload checkpoints.
- **NPU Accelerator Simulation:** For neural acceleration, our implementation generates `SCALE-Sim` configuration files defining array dimensions, dataflow mapping (e.g., Output Stationary vs Weight Stationary), and SRAM scratchpad sizes.
- **Memory System Simulation:** For detailed DRAM memory controller evaluation, our implementation configures `Ramulator` parameter files specifying memory channels, rank/bank timing, and request queue structures.
- **RTL & Gate-Level Simulation:** For hardware verification and physical signoff, our implementation emits SystemVerilog modules compiled via `Verilator` for fast cycle-accurate testing, and gate-level netlists targeting commercial `VCS` flows for exact power and timing extraction.
- **Compiler Transformations:** For software-hardware co-design, our implementation emits TVM/MLIR lowering passes and build scripts that target the specified microarchitecture.

We must also confirm that each tool actually used our requested parameters. A syntactically valid configuration can easily deceive us by selecting the wrong top-level module, reusing stale timing constraints, or skipping the precise workload region that defines our comparison.

This reality highlights a crucial distinction between an infrastructure failure and a candidate failure. If we see a simulator crash, a python syntax error in a `gem5` config, an unparsed key in `SCALE-Sim`, a license timeout in `VCS`, a stale workspace, a malformed timing constraint, an empty netlist, or even a clean tool exit that analyzed zero paths, we only know that our requested test failed to run correctly. These glitches tell us absolutely nothing about the quality of our architectural candidate. Only a valid execution produces a result we can trust to ultimately evaluate or reject a design.

Returning to our XR capacity study, we must translate the 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB capacities into valid requests for both our SRAM timing models and our cycle-level simulators (`gem5`, `SCALE-Sim`, `Ramulator`). If we run an inexpensive SRAM check first, our implementation check must confirm that its area and access-time outputs accurately describe our intended capacity and conditions before we let the evaluation phase use them. While the detailed mechanics of tool isolation, retry, recovery, and interface design belong to environment engineering, our life-cycle handoff is much narrower. Either our intended work ran and produced qualified outputs, or the attempt remains a simple infrastructure failure.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="Multi-tool execution failure misdiagnosed as candidate rejection"}
**The trap.** An automated search agent reports 0.0\ W power, 0.0\ mm^2^ area, and near-zero latency, declaring an NPU/CPU subsystem candidate as an optimal winner.

**The mechanism.** The tool request passed an incompatible parameter flag to `SCALE-Sim` and omitted the primary clock constraint in `VCS`. Elaborators selected an empty top-level stub, simulation completed in zero cycles, gate-level timing analyzed zero paths, and downstream log parsers substituted default zeros for missing power, area, and latency metrics.

**The lesson.** We must recognize this as an infrastructure execution failure, not an architectural breakthrough or a legitimately evaluated candidate. A rigorous implementation check confirms that expected clocks, instances, memory requests, and log outputs actually exist before our evaluation phase interprets their numbers.

We built this composite from recurring tool-flow failure patterns across simulation and EDA toolchains.
:::

### Stage 4: Evaluating Candidate Evidence

We can evaluate a candidate only after checking our implementation record to confirm the intended work actually ran. Once verified, we compare returned measurements against the requirements, objectives, and validity conditions we established during formulation. The outcome provides much more than a simple score. It explicitly details which checks passed, failed, or remain unresolved, and it shows precisely how much confidence our measurements justify.

In our prospective XR subsystem study, we first demand that declared functional regression and coherence checks pass in `Verilator` before applying any hard physical constraints. We reject a subsystem macro outside our 1.5\ mm^2^ area limit, beyond the 2.5\ ns access-time allocation, or above the 3\ W total envelope, even if it drastically improves frame time. A feasible candidate must then face a tail-latency comparison against our rerun 2\ MiB baseline across our cycle-level simulation tools (`gem5`, `SCALE-Sim`, `Ramulator`). We cannot accept a reduction in raw cache or buffer misses as a substitute for a fully resolved frame-time result, because our initial claim targets both the mechanism and the system-level outcome (<7\ ms M2P latency).

As we shape our order of evaluation, we balance tool cost and fidelity across a multi-fidelity evaluation spectrum:

1. **Analytical & Empirical Models:** Fast CACTI SRAM models and analytical roofline estimates filter out candidates that violate fundamental physical area or timing bounds in seconds.
2. **Cycle-Level Subsystem Simulation:** Integrated runs using `SCALE-Sim` (for NPU spatial arrays), `gem5` (for CPU pipelines and cache hierarchies), and `Ramulator` (for DRAM memory controller delays) capture dynamic queueing, contention, and frame-time latency over millions of cycles.
3. **RTL Cycle-Accurate Simulation:** High-speed SystemVerilog simulation in `Verilator` verifies bit-exact functional correctness, ISA compliance, and exact cycle counts for critical kernel blocks.
4. **Gate-Level Synthesis & Power Signoff:** Gate-level simulation in commercial `VCS` paired with static timing and power signoff tools extracts true dynamic/leakage power under gate-level switching activity.

We recognize that a lower-fidelity model (such as an analytical roofline or abstract CACTI estimate) can miss absolute physical values while perfectly preserving the delta, or ranking, between our baseline and candidate. Therefore, we must validate the specific property driving our decision over the relevant region. A single accuracy metric simply cannot establish every kind of comparison we need to make.

While higher fidelity strengthens our answer to the declared question, provided its assumptions and validation support the comparison – it never widens our decision scope. For example, a cycle-level result in `gem5` or `SCALE-Sim` does not authorize full silicon fabrication if our study only promised a recommendation for gate-level RTL evaluation. Similarly, an RTL result from `Verilator` or `VCS` cannot waive the thermal, IR-drop, reliability, or broader product reviews that we intentionally excluded from our study.

Because of these dynamics, our evaluation can end in several legitimate states. When we encounter an invalid execution, we return to the Implement phase; if our comparison lacks required observations, we loop back to Evaluate. Even a completely valid result might simply reject a candidate. In other cases, our measurements may remain too uncertain to distinguish between two candidates, our run budget might expire, or the required data may simply be unavailable. Each of these states demands a different next action, and we must keep them fully visible for subsequent review.

### Stage 5: Interpreting Empirical Results

Even if a favorable number clears all of our declared checks, we might still struggle to explain why the design actually improved. While evaluation simply establishes whether a result passes basic checks, interpretation tells us what the result means. Explanation, in turn, tests whether our proposed hardware-software mechanism truly accounts for that outcome.

Suppose our 3\ MiB subsystem configuration reduces memory stalls and improves 99th-percentile frame time in `gem5` and `SCALE-Sim`. While this result is consistent with our claim, it doesn't establish the underlying mechanism. The larger capacity might also change hit latency, memory-level parallelism, NoC contention, or compiler thread scheduling. When we rely on stable frame identifiers, miss classifications, and relevant telemetry across CPU queues, NPU buffers, and `Ramulator` memory controllers, we can connect our measured outcomes to a concrete physical account rather than just telling a plausible story.

Gupta and colleagues offer a useful warning here. They used an evolutionary coding agent to write last-level cache replacement policies for ChampSim [@GoberEtAl2022ChampSim; @GuptaEtAl2026ArchAgent]. One generated policy appeared to improve instructions per cycle by bypassing writes, which then quietly vanished from the modeled memory system. The simulator score certainly improved, but that gain didn't come from any valid cache mechanism. Only a close inspection of the generated policy and the simulator's behavior exposed the loophole.

Similar simulator loopholes exist across all subsystem domains:
- **NPU Accelerators:** An optimizer in `SCALE-Sim` might appear to achieve 2× throughput by omitting weight buffer sync barriers, causing data hazards that manifest as corrupted visual frames in physical hardware.
- **Memory Controllers:** A scheduling optimization in `Ramulator` might show lower average memory latency by indefinitely starving low-priority background queues, violating real-time display refresh deadlines.
- **Software Compilers:** A compiler pass in TVM or MLIR might eliminate vector spill code in simulation by assuming unconstrained register file capacity, failing when compiled for target hardware in `Verilator`.

This doesn't mean we need an elaborate causal proof for every single result. Rather, it reminds us that improving a metric and proving a mechanism are two entirely different claims. Sometimes, a direct physical check easily explains a simple violation. For more tightly coupled behavior, we might need a contrast, counterfactual, or ablation study. Ultimately, we should match our planned level of explanation to the consequence of the design decision, and to the ways our evaluation setup might be exploited.

Whenever possible, we should choose our required observations before we trigger an expensive run. A top-line score simply cannot recover miss classifications or per-frame histories that the run discarded along the way. In our prospective XR subsystem study, for instance, the expected output is an account of whether reduced memory capacity stalls actually occur in the specific workload frames setting tail latency, and whether they explain the frame-time change. That account might support both the mechanism and the outcome, support just one, or leave both unresolved. Missing observations return us to Evaluate, while a contradicted mechanism sends us back to the claim. While fluent prose can organize our final account, it can never replace the hard measurements that support it, nor can it stretch our results beyond the specific workloads, software compilers, and tools we actually tested.

### Stage 6: Reviewing Decision Handoffs

Review brings our scoped plan and all subsequent work back together. At this stage, we ask whether we explored the legal alternatives adequately, whether our intended tools (`gem5`, `SCALE-Sim`, `Ramulator`, `Verilator`, `VCS`) successfully ran, and whether our measurements satisfy declared checks. We must also verify that our explanation is credible and, ultimately, whether the accumulated work supports our intended decision.

The result is not always an approval. Through our review, we might advance one candidate, reject another, or request an entirely new comparison. We may also revise the original question, narrow our conclusion, or simply stop because we have exhausted our budget or available information. An honest, unresolved result remains a useful outcome as long as our study record clearly explains why the question remains open.

In our prospective XR subsystem study, our review might advance the 3\ MiB or 4\ MiB capacity to gate-level RTL evaluation, or reject both if a declared physical check fails. Alternatively, we might request another comparison if the tail-latency result or our proposed mechanism remains unresolved. If we exhaust our budget before we can support any option, our study stops without a recommendation.

We can close the scoped review only when we have either resolved every required result or explicitly left it unresolved. Our supported action must stay inside the declared scope, and our study record must name what conditions would reopen the work. Closing the study does not authorize a final silicon commitment. Rather, our study stops when our budget, available evidence, or remaining legal alternatives can no longer justify another useful action. We must remember that an exhausted search does not magically become an accepted design.

When a result is missing, we must know whether to propose another candidate, repair a tool run, collect another measurement, or narrow our decision. That choice depends on what each stage of our responsibility received, what it produced, and where our failed work should return (@tbl-stage-contracts).

| **Stage** | **Receives** | **Produces and checks** | **Repair and handoff** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Formulate** | Product intent, a design question, known requirements, and applicable downstream checks. | A scoped plan whose question, comparator, objectives, constraints, conditions, measurements, budget, stop, decision, and exclusions agree. | Repair our question or scope. We hand the plan to Explore without choosing a method prematurely. |
| **Explore** | Our scoped plan, declared legal changes, and any previously established checks. | One or more legal candidates, their selection history, and the limits of our explored region across coupled hardware/software subsystems. | Repair our design space or search approach. We hand a named candidate to Implement, and use checked failures returned by Evaluate to update the candidate set. |
| **Implement** | A candidate, requested tool work, budget, and required inputs across tools (`gem5`, `SCALE-Sim`, `Ramulator`, `Verilator`, `VCS`). | An execution record showing the requested work ran on our intended state, or a recorded infrastructure failure showing that it did not. | Repair our request or tool setup. We hand completed tool returns to Evaluate, and never treat an unevaluated candidate as rejected. |
| **Evaluate** | Completed tool returns, comparator, planned metrics, thresholds, and validity conditions. | A comparison stating which checks passed, failed, or remain unresolved, together with the observations we need for interpretation. | Repair our measurement plan, rerun within budget, or reject the candidate based on a declared check. |
| **Interpret and Explain** | The checked result, proposed mechanism, and retained observations. | An account supported, revised, or contradicted by a declared contrast, ablation, or direct physical reason. | Repair our hypothesis or request missing observations. We hand the result and mechanism status to Review. |
| **Review and Decide** | The scoped plan and study record from all our prior work. | A decision within the declared scope, a narrower conclusion, a named revision, or an honest stop with unresolved questions. | Reopen the work that owns the missing result or close our study. We preserve the reason for the action. |

: **Each responsibility produces an artifact we can inspect.** Our inputs, outputs, and repair paths remain distinct without prescribing a specific model, method, tool interface, or team organization. {#tbl-stage-contracts} tbl-colwidths="[15,25,34,26]"

The most consequential handoff lies between Implement and Evaluate. Here, our execution record must establish that the intended tool work actually ran before we let any number count for or against the candidate. The other stages preserve this same discipline for our plans, candidates, measurements, explanations, and decisions. Through our review, we use these results to identify exactly where any missing work must return.

During review, we can only choose actions within our assigned authority. While our system might propose a candidate, execute a declared test, reject a candidate when a mechanical check fails, or recommend a next step, it cannot override human judgment. Waiving a requirement or committing our project to a costly, irreversible action remains with the specific people responsible for those decisions. Neither our system nor our review activity can enlarge that authority. When our review calls for revision, we must name the responsibility that reopens the task, taking care to preserve the requirements, candidate, tool conditions, and prior results from which the repaired work proceeds.

## Managing Revisions

We do not treat revision as a separate, seventh stage. When we produce an inadequate output, we simply return the work to the responsibility that owns the repair. If we generate a malformed tool request for `SCALE-Sim` or `gem5`, for instance, we route it back to Implement without altering the candidate itself. When we encounter an unexplained frame-time gain, we might return to Evaluate for more observations, or back to Interpret and Explain to run a more rigorous mechanism test. If a product requirement changes, we reopen Formulate.

When these returns happen repeatedly, we rely on a design loop to keep each change tightly connected to our original question and our next decision. We draw on agile RISC-V development and reusable generator-based hardware construction for this iterative approach [@LeeEtAl2016AgileRISCV; @Izraelevitz2017Chisel]. The path we illustrate in @fig-design-loop shows how our scoped study can revisit the responsibility that owns each repair, all while preserving any work that remains valid.

![**Our design loop revisits the life-cycle responsibility that owns each repair.** In a single pass, we carry the outputs of Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret and Explain, and Review and Decide. We return a named repair to the responsible stage, while we push a supported result toward a scoped outcome.](images/F3-design-loop){#fig-design-loop width="82%" fig-alt="Six life-cycle responsibilities shown as our recurrent path through a scoped plan, legal candidate, execution record, checked result, supported account, and next action. Our Review produces either a scoped outcome or a named repair that returns to the responsible stage."}

We start each pass with our current scoped plan and a legal candidate, complete with its selection history. As we run the tool, we add either an execution record or note an infrastructure failure. We use declared checks to turn valid outputs into a measured result, allowing us to determine exactly what mechanism and conclusion those measurements support. During Review, we explicitly name our next action. If we find a result inadequate, we record our return path to show which responsibility must act next and why. For example, rejecting a 4\ MiB capacity candidate might send our work directly back to exploration.

When we conduct parallel work, we must rigorously preserve the same study state. We ensure each branch names the specific study revision it used, and we record our actions and results strictly against that revision. We merge results only after verifying that their assumptions, interfaces, and permitted changes remain perfectly compatible. If we change a shared requirement, model, or compiler interface in one branch, we must revalidate affected results in all other branches. For example, we might use cycle-level simulation in `gem5` to evaluate a 3\ MiB candidate while our implementation prepares the 4\ MiB `VCS` gate-level script, but only if we bind both branches to the identical study revision. We borrow this change-control obligation directly from systems engineering, which requires us to identify exactly what changed and trigger revalidation for any affected requirements, interfaces, and verification results [@NASA2017SystemsEngineeringHandbook].

Machine-learning systems offer us a valuable precedent for tracking these issues. We know that a local component change can spawn hidden dependencies and subtle feedback loops across data, models, and surrounding software [@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden]. In our architecture studies, introducing a new NPU surrogate model can alter which candidates we actually simulate in `SCALE-Sim`, and we might then use those simulator results as the surrogate's next training data. We extend this tracking challenge across costly tool fidelities and straight into physical consequences. While the software lesson exposes the dependency, we still have to prove that our subsystem conclusion survives a jump to a new tool fidelity or physical implementation.

When we keep every result permanently attached to its study revision, we also preserve crucial learning. We can use a rejected subsystem capacity to inform our later work only if we keep its workload, tool versions (`gem5`, `SCALE-Sim`, `Ramulator`, `Verilator`, `VCS`), process assumptions, and failed check firmly attached to the record. When a change invalidates a result, we don't erase the data, but we do prevent that outdated result from silently carrying forward as current evidence.

## Design-Loop Cards

As architects, we already retain our requirements, experiment results, regression and coverage data, signoff reports, issues, and change records in our standard project systems. Our design-loop card isn't meant to replace those systems or dictate a universal format. Instead, we use it to provide a compact index into the specific artifacts that bear on a single, scoped architecture question and the decision our work is meant to support.

We borrow the core reporting instinct behind model cards and datasheets for datasets, tools that make intended use, evaluation conditions, and known limits readily reviewable [@MitchellEtAl2019ModelCards; @GebruEtAl2021Datasheets]. However, we recognize that this analogy has its limits. Because our designs evolve rapidly, our architecture studies must also preserve the changing design state, tool conditions, physical assumptions, failed checks, and the explicit authority for the next action. A static description of a model or dataset simply cannot carry those responsibilities by itself.

To manage these dynamic requirements, we need a study record that makes our architectural state and its revisions fully inspectable.

> **Study record.** The cumulative account of one scoped architecture study.
> It retains the plan, stage outputs, failed or unevaluated work, unresolved
> questions, stopping reason, and supported decision, with links to the
> detailed artifacts needed for review or replay.

For every consequential transition, our study record explicitly names the revision. It details exactly who or what proposed and approved the action, what executed it across our tool flows (`gem5`, `SCALE-Sim`, `Ramulator`, `Verilator`, `VCS`), what checked the result, and what later change might invalidate it. When we keep our links to existing engineering artifacts current, we avoid blindly copying their contents. We can look to scientific workflow preservation for a strong precedent here; it routinely binds an analysis to versioned inputs, software, parameters, and provenance so another researcher can confidently inspect or replay it [@ChenEtAl2016CERNAnalysisPreservation]. While our architecture work certainly demands that same replayable information, we must go further: we also have to capture the specific decision being supported, the physical assumptions and failed checks that bound our results, and the named authority empowered to act on them.

To be truly useful, this index must directly connect our overarching project goals and constraints to our specific comparisons, tool work, returns, findings, and next actions. We establish this critical connection through a scoped study (@fig-structured-layer-above-rtl).

![**Our scoped architecture study connects intent to implementation evidence.** The study container binds our question and decision to the scope, claim, linked artifacts, tool returns, supported finding, limits, and named owner.](images/F4d-structured-layer-above-rtl){#fig-structured-layer-above-rtl width="85%" fig-alt="Three-layer diagram showing our architecture intent and judgment above a scoped architecture study container. The container connects our question and decision, scope and claim, linked artifacts, tool returns, supported finding, limits, and named owner. Returns from all our implementation tools join a common path back to the study, and later results may revise our claim or study."}

While our project requirements, models, and overarching rationale set the high-level goals, constraints, and stakes, they rarely tell us something as concrete as which specific subsystem capacities we should compare. That's why we use the study question to pinpoint the exact comparison, while our intended decision explains precisely why we are running it. From there, we rely on the scope and architectural claim to explicitly declare what our results must test.

Our study then tightly binds our methods and tool returns directly to that claim. We lean on cycle-level simulators (`gem5`, `SCALE-Sim`, `Ramulator`) to evaluate architectural behavior, while our compilers (TVM/MLIR) and runtimes expose critical software interactions, and our RTL generators produce executable implementations. Finally, we turn to RTL and gate-level EDA flows (`Verilator`, `VCS`) to assess physical properties and exact execution. Ultimately, the returns from all four of these tool families flow back into our study, allowing us to judge the supported finding against our original question, constraints, and known tool limits.

We must remember that a raw tool output is not, by itself, a decision. For a finding to be genuinely supported, it requires explicit limits and a designated owner who is responsible for the next action. If our results suddenly expose a faulty assumption or highlight an underspecified comparison, we step back and deliberately revise our study question or claim; we never allow disconnected tool outputs to blindly stand in for our professional engineering judgment.

We've provided our design-loop card in @fig-filled-design-loop-card as an optional, highly compact index into that study record. We intentionally keep this filled example focused on our ongoing XR subsystem capacity study, rather than muddying the waters by introducing a second, unrelated design problem.

![**Our optional study card separates support from decision.** Our cache example connects intent and scope to our methods, checks, results, and rejected alternatives. Its final row keeps what our evidence supports safely separate from the accountable decision.](images/F4b-design-loop-card-example){#fig-filled-design-loop-card width="84%" fig-alt="Our optional filled study card for the XR capacity comparison. A claim under review appears above entries for the 2 MiB baseline, 3 MiB and 4 MiB candidates, direct enumeration, tool and feedback conditions, failed runs, rejection checks, evidence support, and the accountable decision."}

Our claim at the top clearly anchors the specific entries below it. We use the middle rows to track the work we've planned or already performed, taking care to cleanly distinguish mere infrastructure failures from candidates that were legitimately rejected by our declared checks. We reserve the final row to keep our evidence-based support firmly separated from the accountable decision itself. When we organize it this way, we ensure an unresolved comparison or a budget-driven halt remains plainly visible, rather than quietly recasting it as a completed decision. Ultimately, we treat this card as just one compact view of our study record; it is not a mandatory artifact, nor should it ever substitute for our carefully linked engineering records.

## Open Questions

Our six-stage life cycle succeeds by isolating failures and preserving design intent, yet pushing this discipline to production scale immediately surfaces unresolved tensions where human judgment collides with automated volume. The frontier of our research lies exactly in this collision. While we know AI can generate thousands of candidates and encounter countless infrastructure failures, we still lack scalable principles to determine which fractured state we must preserve for review and which we can cleanly discard. These aren't mere implementation artifacts; they are fundamental research problems. We must figure out how to maintain a reviewable state without drowning in logging, how to dynamically scale our evidence standards as design commitments harden, and how to verify automated explanations when the same underlying model generates both the candidate and its justification. Resolving these challenges is essential to making automated design both ambitious and accountable, and they offer profound structural problems well worth a PhD thesis or dedicated research paper.

**Repair and reviewable state.** When our studies encounter multiple failures across different responsibilities, we have to decide where to start repairs and which parts of the failed work we should keep around for later review.

- **How do we route repair when several life-cycle responsibilities fail simultaneously?** If we just fix the most obvious symptom, like a simulator crash in `gem5` or `SCALE-Sim`, we risk triggering another expensive but invalid run while deeper issues, such as a malformed design candidate or illegal memory constraint, remain untouched. Our goal is to minimize wasted compute cycles and time-to-valid-result without simply papering over the underlying failures.

- **Which failed attempts actually matter for the reviewable state of an AI-assisted study?** If we discard all failures, we lose the context of *why* we avoided certain paths, and we invite the AI, or ourselves, to repeat those exact mistakes. On the other hand, if we keep every broken script or hallucinated candidate, our repositories become unnavigable. We need principled ways to judge what we should retain, balancing the cost of review against the value of documenting the conditions that triggered our failures.

**Proportionate structure and independent review.** We need a life cycle that catches silent drift in our design questions and ensures credible review, but we cannot demand tapeout-level rigor for every early-stage exploration.

- **What evidence can catch silent changes to the design question as a study progresses?** As we move from defining goals to running RTL flows in `Verilator` and `VCS`, our comparator, workload, constraints, or acceptance conditions can slowly drift. Our artifacts might still look compatible, but they no longer answer the original question. We need mechanisms to spot these material shifts early, without forcing us to restart the entire study for every minor tweak.

- **How should the life cycle scale as an architecture decision gets more expensive or harder to reverse?** A quick pathfinding exploration shouldn't require the same heavy records and review as a firm commitment to silicon. Our open problem is how we gracefully strengthen our evidence and review standards as the consequences grow, without losing traceability or bogging ourselves down in unnecessary overhead.

- **How do we review a study when the same AI proposed the candidates, ran the measurements, and wrote the explanation?** Even if we use separate prompts or give the AI different personas, they often share the same underlying model, context window, and blind spots. Our research challenge lies in defining which responsibility boundaries truly need independent verification or human decision rights, and understanding how enforcing that separation impacts both our missed error rate and the cost of our review.

### Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Isolate failure domains to enable targeted repair"}
**Principle:** We must structure our AI-assisted design life cycle so that independently failing outputs belong to distinct responsibilities.

**Rationale:** When our components fail independently, we must keep their repairs cleanly decoupled.

**Action:** Route any inadequate result directly back to the responsibility that owns its repair. We must preserve our original design questions, selected candidates, tool configurations, and valid prior results to prevent redundant computation and state corruption.
:::

Our AI-assisted design life cycle keeps the entire path, from our initial intent all the way to a reviewed architecture decision, highly coherent. As architects, we turn a broad goal into testable requirements, objectives, legal alternatives, and an intended decision, and then we find candidates inside that space. Our simulators (`gem5`, `SCALE-Sim`, `Ramulator`), compilers (TVM, MLIR), RTL flows (`Verilator`), and gate-level EDA tools (`VCS`) make those candidates testable, while execution checks help us separate valid work from infrastructure failure. Declared checks qualify our results, and we connect them directly to an architectural mechanism and its limits before deciding whether to advance, reject, revise, or stop.

We treat these responsibilities as neither a rigid waterfall nor a black-box agent architecture. Instead, we can repeat, overlap, and return to them whenever our work needs repair. We design this process to prevent different failures from collapsing into a single unsuccessful run. For us, a malformed tool invocation is not a rejected design. A favorable score is not a substitute for an explanation. A higher-fidelity measurement does not grant broader authority. And a budget stop is never a completed decision.

In our prospective XR subsystem example, we saw how a tightly scoped study uses this complete life cycle. We translated our broad system goal into a narrow decision about which subsystem capacity, if any, we should advance to gate-level RTL evaluation. We kept hard constraints strictly separate from tradeoff objectives, and we ensured our tail latency stayed connected to real-time workload deadlines (<7\ ms M2P target). Before any single metric could reject a candidate, our tool requests had to establish that the intended design actually ran. Ultimately, our final study record preserved our open questions and decision limits up front, rather than filling them in after the fact.

Bringing AI assistance into our workflows increases the need to preserve our design intent as our work crosses models, methods, software, hardware descriptions, simulators, and physical tools. This life cycle gives us, alongside our automated methods and engineering tools, a common structure for those handoffs. We can push more work forward without ever letting the speed or fluency of the system substitute for our own engineering judgment.

That structure can only operate when our study has usable data, current project knowledge, and representations that preserve the design relationships our work depends on. We develop those requirements in @sec-data-representations-world-models, without assuming that any single representation can serve us across every stage.
